strengths: Addresses an important and realistic offline-to-online RL setting: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment non-curated data for online RL.
Large-scale empirical evaluation on 72 tasks across 6 embodiments (DMControl and Meta-World), with 3 seeds and full per-task results in the appendix.
Shows substantial sample-efficiency gains: 102.8% relative improvement over learning-from-scratch baselines at 150k samples and strong performance on hard exploration tasks.
Ablations and follow-up experiments support the roles of world-model pre-training, experience rehearsal, execution guidance, and fine-tuning different world-model components.
The proposed techniques are practical: they require no reward labels or expert demonstrations and can be integrated with standard RSSM-based world models.
Includes detailed hyperparameters, compute resources, limitations, and implementation details, which helps contextualize the empirical claims.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: experience rehearsal largely retrieves and replays offline data, which is conceptually related to RLPD/ExPLORe, while execution guidance is close to JSRL/behavior-cloning priors with a modified switching schedule.
The world-model architecture is a standard RSSM with minor engineering changes (zero-padded actions, larger scale), not a methodological advance.

The theoretical analysis is weak and partly unsound: Proposition 1 assumes retrieval based on initial observations guarantees all retrieved states are close to online states; Proposition 2 asserts a regularizer prevents forgetting without formal conditions; Proposition 3 assumes the guide policy has positive advantage over the current policy for all states, which is generally false.

The 'non-curated' claim is somewhat overstated: the offline data is still generated within DMControl/Meta-World from known task distributions and pre-trained agents, with added noise, rather than truly in-the-wild or arbitrary internet-scale data.

The abstract claim of matching baselines trained with larger budgets is not fully supported: on Meta-World, GSA at 150k obtains mean success 0.750 vs Dreamer v3 at 1M at 0.900, and it is substantially worse on some individual tasks.

The distribution-shift motivation is supported mainly by a single task visualization (Shelf Place) and Wasserstein distances; it does not quantify how prevalent the issue is across the 72 evaluated tasks.

Retrieval uses only initial-observation features, so it may fail to identify trajectories that are dynamically relevant but start from slightly different states; no sensitivity analysis is provided for retrieval size, feature choice, or top-k.

Baseline tuning and comparison may be incomplete: ExPLORe and JSRL-BC are adapted variants, and the baselines receive task-filtered offline data while GSA uses multi-embodiment data, making it unclear how much of the gain comes from relative tuning versus methodology.

Reproducibility is challenging: the approach uses a 280M-parameter model, a 10M state-action offline dataset, and roughly 1728 GPU hours for the main results; no released code or checkpoints are mentioned.
Execution guidance relies on task-specific schedules and hyperparameters, but no thorough sensitivity study is provided to show robustness across tasks.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data to improve online RL sample efficiency.
Provides a large-scale empirical evaluation across 72 visuomotor tasks and 6 embodiments, which is substantially broader than many prior offline-to-online RL and world-model papers.
The proposed GSA pipeline is technically plausible and mostly clearly described, with hyperparameters, algorithm details, and compute resources reported.
Ablation studies on pre-training, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance give some evidence that the components contribute to performance.
Shows strong aggregate improvements over learning-from-scratch baselines and some offline-data baselines on several hard locomotion and manipulation tasks.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: experience rehearsal is essentially nearest-neighbor retrieval plus replay of offline data, and execution guidance is a JSRL/behavior-cloning-style prior with random mid-episode switching. The combination is engineering-driven rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution for a top-tier AI conference.

The central claim that naive world-model fine-tuning fails mainly due to distributional shift is not rigorously established. The evidence is largely qualitative t-SNE visualization on one task plus Wasserstein distances, without broad causal analysis across the 72 tasks.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is weak. Proposition 1 is essentially tautological under the assumption that retrieval selects close states; Proposition 2 is informal and relies on hand-wavy regularization assumptions; Proposition 3 adopts a TRPO-style coupled-policy bound under a strong and likely unrealistic assumption that the behavior-cloning guide has positive advantage everywhere early in training.

Evaluation fairness is not fully convincing. The iVideoGPT comparison uses numbers from another paper under potentially different settings, task suites, and training tricks. The manuscript claims GSA matches baselines trained with 3.3-6.7x more samples, but on Meta-World Dreamer v3 at 1M has mean success 0.900 versus GSA at 150k with 0.750, so the claim is overbroad.

Retrieval is based only on initial-observation similarity using the pre-trained encoder, with no quantitative validation of retrieval relevance or sensitivity to top-k. In multi-task and multi-embodiment settings, initial observations can be ambiguous, so retrieved trajectories may not be task-relevant.

The behavior-cloning prior is trained on retrieved mixed-quality, noisy offline data, yet the method relies on this prior for execution guidance. There is little analysis of how mixed quality affects the prior policy or why the fixed switching schedule is robust across tasks.

Important ablations are missing: no comparison against simply replaying all offline data or a random offline subset, no study of retrieval granularity/metrics, no analysis of action zero-padding across embodiments, and no scaling analysis of model size or offline data size.
Reproducibility is a concern. No code or dataset release is mentioned, and the compute cost is very high (roughly 1728 GPU hours for main results), making independent verification difficult.
The paper contains several presentation issues and overclaims, including typos such as "Meta-Wolrd" and repeated claims that are stronger than the evidence presented.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: improving sample efficiency of online RL by using reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data.
The proposed GSA pipeline is clear and practical: generalist world-model pre-training, retrieval-based experience rehearsal, and BC-based execution guidance.
The empirical evaluation is extensive: 72 visuomotor tasks across 6 embodiments, comparisons with multiple offline-data and learning-from-scratch baselines, and 3 seeds per task.
The reported gains at a limited online budget are substantial, especially on several hard exploration and manipulation tasks, and the ablations support the importance of both rehearsal and guidance.
The paper provides detailed implementation, hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, and compute resources, which improves transparency.
The problem analysis around distribution shift between offline pre-training and online fine-tuning is useful and motivates the proposed techniques well.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the approach largely combines existing ideas (RSSM world models, retrieval, replay of offline data, JSRL-style policy guidance, and BC) rather than introducing a fundamentally new technique.

The 'non-curated' offline-data claim is somewhat overstated: the data is in-domain and task-related, generated by pre-trained RL/unsupervised agents, and in Meta-World includes target-task near-expert trajectories with injected noise. This makes it unclear how much of the gain comes from generalist world-model dynamics versus target-task demonstration retrieval and BC guidance.

Some claims are not fully supported by the results: GSA at 150k does not clearly match Dreamer v3 at 1M on Meta-World (0.750 vs. 0.900 mean success), despite the abstract suggesting it matches larger-budget baseline performance.
The theoretical analysis is superficial and largely tautological/informal; it does not meaningfully justify the main algorithmic design or provide non-trivial insights.

Baseline comparisons may not be fully conclusive: ExPLORe and JSRL-BC are modified/tuned under the authors' setting, iVideoGPT results are taken from prior work with different experiment details, and there is no ablation comparing retrieval-based rehearsal against random replay or full-dataset replay.
Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a code release and by substantial compute requirements (hundreds of GPU hours for the main experiments).
The method is evaluated only in simulation, and the paper acknowledges that in-the-wild or real-world transfer remains untested.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data to improve online RL sample efficiency.
Identifies distributional shift between offline pre-training and online fine-tuning as a key failure mode, with useful t-SNE/Wasserstein visualization and analysis.
Proposes two simple, complementary techniques—experience rehearsal via retrieval and execution guidance via a prior policy—that are well motivated and ablated.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 72 tasks and 6 embodiments, with multiple seeds, full result tables, and comparisons to from-scratch, offline-data, model-based, and continual-learning baselines.
Demonstrates substantial sample-efficiency gains, especially on hard exploration and robotic manipulation tasks, often matching baselines trained with far more environment steps.
Provides good reproducibility details: algorithm, hyperparameters, compute resources, implementation notes, and limitations.
Clear positioning relative to prior work (offline RL, offline-to-online RL, world model pre-training, representation learning, generalist agents).
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the approach largely combines existing ideas—RSSM world-model pre-training, nearest-neighbor retrieval/replay, and behavior-cloning-based guided exploration—rather than introducing fundamentally new techniques.

The theoretical analysis is relatively shallow: Proposition 1 relies on the assumption that retrieved states are closer to online states, and Proposition 2 is a direct application of existing Kakade & Langford results; the catastrophic-forgetting argument is informal.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing: some baselines are modified or may not be optimally tuned for the non-curated multi-embodiment setting, and the iVideoGPT comparison partly uses reported results or different pre-training setups.

The claim of using 'non-curated' data is somewhat overstated: the datasets are still in-domain and generated by specific RL agents, not truly in-the-wild or naturally noisy human-collected data, as the limitations section acknowledges.

Aggregate performance improvements are clear, but on Meta-World DrQ-v2 at 1M samples slightly exceeds NCRL in mean success rate, and several individual tasks show worse performance; claims should be more carefully qualified.

Execution guidance depends on the quality of the offline data and the BC prior, but the paper mostly assumes the prior is beneficial early on; this assumption may not always hold for mixed-quality data.

No real-world robot experiments, and the proposed retrieval strategy is based only on initial-observation similarity, which may be brittle in tasks with similar initial states but different required behaviors.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: improving sample efficiency in RL by leveraging offline data that is reward-free, mixed-quality, and multi-embodiment.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering 72 visuomotor tasks across DMControl and Meta-World, with multiple baselines including DrQ-v2, DreamerV3, R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT, and PackNet.
The identification of distributional shift between offline pre-training data and online fine-tuning data is well motivated and empirically visualized through t-SNE and Wasserstein distance analyses.

The proposed combination of experience rehearsal and execution guidance is shown to improve performance across many challenging tasks, and the ablation studies help isolate the contribution of each component.
Reproducibility is reasonably strong: the paper includes implementation details, hyperparameters, compute resources, full algorithm, and extensive appendix results.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with a coherent pipeline and useful comparisons to prior offline-to-online RL and world model pre-training methods.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. The main components—RSSM-based world model pre-training, retrieval-based experience rehearsal, and behavior-cloning-based execution guidance—are largely combinations or extensions of existing ideas (DreamerV3, RLPD, JSRL, ExPLORe). The paper does not introduce a fundamentally new algorithm or theoretical insight.

The central claim of using 'non-curated' offline data is overstated. For Meta-World, the offline dataset is collected using task-specific TDMPC-v2 agents with injected Gaussian noise across the same 50 tasks that are later evaluated, meaning the offline data contains task-relevant, near-expert trajectories for the downstream tasks. This is not as 'non-curated' as claimed, and makes the experimental setting closer to reward-free but still task-specific offline RL.

The multi-embodiment aspect is not convincingly evaluated. The method trains separate world models per benchmark rather than a single model across all six embodiments, and there is no ablation isolating whether multi-embodiment pre-training actually helps compared to single-embodiment pre-training.

The theoretical analysis in the appendix is shallow and largely standard. Proposition 1 mainly states that selecting closer points reduces average distance, and Proposition 2 is a direct application of Kakade & Langford (2002). These do not provide meaningful new theoretical support for the method.

The evaluation does not test truly out-of-distribution or cross-task generalization where the offline data lacks trajectories for the downstream task. The retrieval mechanism may succeed largely because task-specific trajectories exist in the offline dataset, which limits the strength of the claim that non-curated data can be broadly leveraged.

Some quantitative comparisons weaken the claimed margin. In Meta-World, NCRL at 150k steps achieves a mean success rate of 0.748 versus DrQ-v2 at 1M steps at 0.753, so NCRL matches but does not clearly surpass a well-tuned baseline when given enough samples. The sample-efficiency claim is stronger than the final-performance claim.

The execution guidance component relies on a behavior-cloned prior from retrieved data, but its benefit depends on π_bc outperforming π_rl early in training. This assumption is not deeply validated across tasks, and the random mid-episode switching schedule may be sensitive in ways not fully ablated.

The paper lacks important ablations on data scale, data quality, retrieval robustness, and what happens when the offline dataset is genuinely unrelated to the target task. Without these, the scope and limitations of the method remain unclear.
The ethics and broader-impact discussion is generic and does not specifically address risks of deploying RL agents trained with large-scale offline data or potential biases in non-curated datasets.

strengths: Addresses a practical and under-explored offline-to-online RL setting with reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment data.
Extensive empirical evaluation: 72 tasks across Meta-World and DMControl, 6 embodiments, multiple seeds, many baselines, ablations, and continual adaptation.
Clear diagnosis of distribution shift between pretraining and online fine-tuning, with concrete visual/quantitative evidence and simple mitigation techniques.
Experience rehearsal and execution guidance are simple, well-motivated, and consistently improve sample efficiency; results often match or exceed baselines trained with much larger sample budgets.
Good reproducibility details (hyperparameters, compute, algorithm, implementation descriptions) and fair attention to limitations.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: task-agnostic RSSM pretraining, retrieval/replay, and behavioral-cloning guidance are largely existing components; the main contribution is a combination/recipe.

Theoretical analysis is weak and somewhat overstated; Proposition 1 assumes retrieval selects states close to online states, whereas the method retrieves trajectories using only initial-observation encoder distance, and Proposition 2 directly cites an existing result.

Comparison protocols are not fully apples-to-apples: baselines are given task-relevant/curated trajectories while NCRL uses non-curated multi-embodiment data, and missing ablations compare retrieval against random replay or full-offline replay at similar budget.
Retrieval quality depends on a single initial observation and can degrade on some tasks (e.g., Door Open precision drops), with no robust fallback or more principled trajectory-matching objective.

The paper claims a multi-embodiment world model, but trains separate models per benchmark and Meta-World uses a single embodiment; the cross-embodiment generalization claim is therefore somewhat weaker than stated.
Theoretical claims about reducing distribution shift and preventing catastrophic forgetting are not rigorously tied to the actual algorithm.
